intro: A clarinet melody in two beats takes the place of a headlong scherzo. The middle changes to 6/8 and the distant key of B major; its repeated-note rhythm survives inside the opening material’s return.
question: What remains of the middle section when the opening melody comes back?

cues.title: An Allegretto, not a scherzo
cues.text: Brahms asks for a moderately quick, graceful movement in two beats. Clarinets begin the melody over plucked cellos, with bassoon and horn support. The lighter scoring and measured pace distinguish this movement from a driving Beethovenian scherzo.
cues.evidence: The first-edition score p. 35 shows the 2/4 heading, clarinet melody and pizzicato cello accompaniment. The report begins quietly and rises across 0:00–0:15; the observation concerns the opening passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A phrase turned upside down
cues.text: The opening melody’s answering phrase reverses its direction: rises become falls and falls become rises. Listen for that relationship rather than expecting a completely different answer. The theme can change shape while retaining its interval pattern.
cues.evidence: The score’s first two five-bar phrases are related by melodic inversion, also described in Hansen’s guide. This note invites comparison across the opening section; it does not identify the first inverted note at 0:35.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A pattern for later symphonies
cues.text: Brahms followed the long-delayed First with his Second Symphony in 1877. Its third movement also uses a moderate, graceful pace as its starting point; the First’s compact interlude was not an isolated solution to the symphonic scherzo position.
cues.evidence: The site’s Brahms biography gives the Second Symphony’s 1877 date. Mandel compares the graceful third movements: https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor

cues.title: The trio changes the subdivision
cues.text: In the middle section, the beat divides into three rather than two. Repeated wind notes answer descending string arpeggios in 6/8, and B major replaces A♭. The contrast involves rhythm and tonal distance as well as a different melody.
cues.evidence: Bar 71 begins the B-major 6/8 trio. A boundary at 1:42 and the changed pitch region at 1:40–1:55 support approximate placement at 102 seconds; the written key and metre come from the score, not the report’s key labels.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The middle gains orchestral weight
cues.text: The trio’s repeated notes and descending figures grow into a stronger orchestral stretch. Listen for the way the same exchange can support a larger swell without losing its short, recognisable gestures.
cues.evidence: The score expands the trio’s repeated-note and arpeggio pattern through bars 87–108. Relative level rises from −16.0 dB at 1:50 to −5.4 at 2:20, then remains comparatively high; this supports the broad buildup.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The middle movements divided listeners
cues.text: The conductor Hermann Levi thought the symphony’s two middle movements out of place beside its expansive outer movements. His objection identifies a real contrast of scale: this Allegretto is less than five minutes in the present recording.
cues.evidence: Mandel reports Levi’s judgement: https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor. The cached analysis gives this file as 295.0 seconds; the duration is a recording measurement, not a claim about every performance.

cues.title: The trio survives the return
cues.text: The opening melody returns, but wind triplets preserve the trio’s repeated-note figure above it. Two earlier textures now coexist. Listen for a familiar tune acquiring a new rhythmic companion instead of replacing the middle section completely.
cues.evidence: The score restores 2/4 at bar 109 and the opening tune at bar 115, keeping the trio figure as triplets. The report’s strongest boundary at 3:16 precedes the lower-level stretch at 3:20–3:35; the return is estimated at 3:28.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A symphony for four hands
cues.text: Simrock published Brahms’s own piano-duet arrangement alongside the orchestral score in October 1877. Two pianists could therefore study the symphony’s changing lines and rhythms at one keyboard, without assembling an orchestra.
cues.evidence: The Brahms-Institut catalogue identifies the October 1877 full score, plate 7957, and the composer’s piano-four-hands arrangement, plate 7959: https://brahmsinstitut.de/Archiv/web/bihl_digital/jb_werkekatalog/op_068.html

cues.title: The middle becomes an ending
cues.text: The coda recalls the trio’s repeated notes and descending broken chords, now gently and in the home-key surroundings. Brahms marks the close progressively more tranquil; the earlier contrast becomes material for bringing the movement to rest.
cues.evidence: Bars 154–164 reuse trio material under poco a poco più tranquillo. The report has boundaries at 4:20–4:24 and 4:38, and falls to −30.2 dB at 4:50 before the 295-second end. Individual slowing points are not measured.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: One pitch opens a distant key
transitions.how: The end of the opening section slows into an E♭-centred preparation. That pitch can be respelled D♯, the third of B major, allowing the music to enter a distant key without an unrelated starting note. The metre changes from 2/4 to 6/8: repeated wind notes and descending string broken chords replace the opening’s longer clarinet line.
transitions.evidence: The written join is at bar 71, described in Hansen’s guide. The report changes around 1:42 after an E♭-weighted span at 1:30–1:35. The enharmonic reading is score-derived; 102 seconds is approximate.

transitions.title: The trio’s rhythm crosses the bar line
transitions.how: The trio’s cadential energy subsides, with D♯/E♭ again serving as a connecting pitch. Strings anticipate the opening theme in A♭ minor as the notation returns to 2/4. Winds continue the trio’s repeated notes as triplets, preserving the old subdivision inside the new metre. A quieter plucked descent then prepares the restoration of A♭ major.
transitions.evidence: Bars 109–114 supply the retransition. The report’s strongest boundary occurs at 3:16, with relative level falling through 3:20–3:25, supporting the broad join at 196 seconds.

transitions.title: The old melody keeps a new companion
transitions.how: The clarinet melody and plucked cello foundation recover the opening’s A♭ major, but flutes and oboes retain the trio’s repeated-note triplets above them. Brahms brings back only a shortened opening section, omitting its contrasting inner episode. The return therefore combines two previously separate ideas and changes the proportions at the same time.
transitions.evidence: Bar 115 begins the reprise, with the trio figure carried over. The report’s lower-level region at 3:20–3:35 and a boundary at 3:28 support the approximate 208-second anchor, not a precisely timed clarinet entry.

transitions.title: An avoided close recalls the trio
transitions.how: The returning section approaches a cadence, then continues with the trio’s repeated notes and broken chords instead of stopping. Their new quietness and the instruction poco a poco più tranquillo change their function: what supplied contrast in the middle now prolongs the ending. The harmony briefly touches D♭ before moving back towards the final A♭ cadence.
transitions.evidence: The coda starts at bar 154 in the score. The 4:20 and 4:24 boundaries, followed by a quieter span at 4:25–4:35, support its estimated placement at 264 seconds.

source.title: Brahms, Symphony No. 1, Simrock first-edition full score, plate 7957 (1877)
source.locator: Movement III, pp. 35–42. Opening inspected directly; later textures follow Hansen’s bar descriptions at 45, 71, 87, 109, 115 and 154. No timpani, contrabassoon or trombones in this movement. Entries are representative passage snapshots with approximate timing.

timeline.note: Clarinet melody above plucked cellos, with bassoon and horn harmony.
The opening tune passes to violins while clarinet adds a triplet counterline.
The opening section’s more active inner episode combines wind melody with divided string pulsation.
In the trio, repeated wind notes alternate with descending string broken chords.
The expanded trio gains trumpet support above active string arpeggios.
Strings anticipate the opening while winds retain the trio’s repeated-note pattern.
The clarinet-led reprise shares the foreground with the trio’s upper-wind triplets.
Quiet string and wind exchanges recall the trio’s pattern in the coda.

composer.background:
Brahms was born in Hamburg, the son of a professional musician, Johann Jakob Brahms, who played several instruments, and Christiane Nissen, a seamstress. His father supplied an introduction to practical music-making; Otto Friedrich Willibald Cossel and Eduard Marxsen gave him systematic piano and composition lessons. The young Brahms played for income and learned the trade from inside, accompanying, arranging and performing. Marxsen’s teaching connected keyboard technique with the study of Bach, Mozart and Beethoven. Those composers supplied working materials: Brahms’s later scores are full of old procedures subjected to new rhythmic pressure.

In 1853 he toured with the Hungarian violinist Ede Reményi and met Joseph Joachim, who became a lifelong collaborator. Joachim sent him to Robert and Clara Schumann in Düsseldorf. Robert’s article “Neue Bahnen”, published that October, announced the twenty-year-old as a major new figure before his music was widely available. The endorsement opened publishers’ doors and imposed an awkward expectation of scale. His early piano sonatas, already orchestral in weight and contrast, could be treated as promises of symphonies he had not yet written. Brahms responded by publishing selectively and destroying much of the work he did not wish to preserve.
composer.epithet: A composer who made a small interval generate a large form, and let conflicting rhythms keep a familiar melody unsettled.
